description: Per-translation glossary overlay for the Wheel of Heaven Translation of the Ōmoto Shin'yu (大本神諭, Divine Revelations), chapter 1 = the Meiji 25 (1892) founding oracles of Deguchi Nao (the first fude, old-cal. 1st month; and old-cal. 5th month 5th day), OSHIN-1:1…OSHIN-1:93. This is the pipeline's first Japanese-source text; the central production glossary is Semitic-only and covers no Japanese lemmata, so every Ōmoto-technical lexical decision is logged here. Contains: the Hepburn-romanization convention scoped to this text; the ぞよ (zo yo) oracular-ender rendering policy; the standing theonym 艮の金神 (Ushitora no Konjin) with its 国常立尊 (Kunitokotachi) identification; 三千世界 (sanzen sekai) the Buddhist trichiliocosm; 立替へ立直し (tatekae-tatenaoshi) the reconstruction-and-renewal eschatology; 改心 (kaishin) 'change of heart'; the NEUTRAL rendering of 神 (kami) by the text's own theism; 神国 (shinkoku) 'divine land'; the 神柱/守護神/守護人 (kamibashira/shugojin/shugonin) guardian hierarchy; the lacuna-marker (○○○［) house convention; the 金輪王 (konrin'ō) + Takamagahara / Ryūmonkan / ikigami mythic-toponym set; the 大本 (Ōmoto) site-vs-'great-origin' split; the 出口直 (Deguchi Nao) name/adverb pun; the sensitive-register (xenophobic/ableist) accuracy-first-plus-contextualize policy; the 水晶魂 (crystal soul) soul-purification vocabulary; and the reikaimonogatari.net collation-witness framework with its partial (38/93) match and the 一同/一度 orthographic variant. The English is an independent scholarly translation. NOTE: one proposed entry — the interpretive identification of Ōmoto's banished-and-returning creator-kami (Ushitora no Konjin / Kunitokotachi) with the Wheel of Heaven Elohim frame — is claim_type=speculative and is NOT included here; per the ratified Hidden Words b-h-y ruling of 2026-07-03 the surface text is kept NEUTRAL and the resonance lives in comparative commentary only. That speculative entry is escalated to the human reviewer in chapter-1-editor-report.md pending explicit sign-off. A single-edition philological pass against an authoritative Ōmoto Shin'yu edition is still pending (see the collation entry).

entries.lemma: the project-specific romanization convention for the Japanese source text of the Ōmoto Shin'yu: modified (revised) Hepburn — long vowels by macron (ō ū; ā ī where they occur); syllabic ん as n (n' before a vowel or y, e.g. Ushitora no Konjin, sanzen, shin'yu); geminate consonants doubled (tatekae, Ryūmonkan, matsu); し/ち/つ/ふ as shi/chi/tsu/fu; を as wo only where it is the object particle in the running transliteration; proper nouns capitalized; the sentence-final particle-cluster ぞよ transliterated 'zo yo'. Historical kana orthography (歴史的仮名遣い) in the source (現はれて, 治まらん, 行けぬ, 致すぞよ) is read at its modern phonemic value (arawarete, osamaran, ikenu, itasu zo yo)
entries.standardEnglish: modified/revised Hepburn (the Library of Congress and academic standard) as the project standard for Japanese-source romanization
entries.wohChoice: the translit field reflects modified Hepburn with macron long vowels and phonemic reading of historical kana; this entry scopes that convention to the Ōmoto Shin'yu (OSHIN-WOH) as the pipeline's first Japanese-source text
entries.rationale: The Ōmoto Shin'yu is the first Japanese-source text in the Translation Program, and no romanization convention was previously scoped for Japanese, so the translit field's scheme must be ratified and documented for auditability. Modified (revised) Hepburn is the academic and library standard (the ALA-LC Japanese Romanization Table; Kenkyusha's New Japanese-English Dictionary; the Nihongo daijiten), distinct from Kunrei-shiki (si/ti/tu) and from Nihon-shiki, and it is the scheme a scholarly reader of romanized Japanese expects. A specific sub-decision is recorded: the source carries pre-reform historical kana orthography (歴史的仮名遣い, e.g. 現はれて for arawarete, 了ふ for shimau), which the transliteration reads at its modern phonemic value rather than transliterating the obsolete kana letter-for-letter, because the target is a pronunciation-faithful reading aid, not a paleographic reconstruction of Meiji orthography. Named references: the ALA-LC Romanization Tables (Library of Congress); J. C. Hepburn, A Japanese-English and English-Japanese Dictionary (1886); the Kenkyusha standard. Promotion candidate: to be promoted to the central glossary as a project-wide convention if further Japanese-source texts adopt it.

entries.lemma: ぞよ (zo yo), the sentence-final particle cluster (emphatic ぞ + emotive/vocative よ) that ends the great majority of the 93 verses. In the archaic, oracular register of Deguchi Nao's fude it marks the whole text as emphatic, assertive, first-person divine speech — a fixed cadence of the kami's voice — with no close English equivalent
entries.literal: [emphatic-assertive sentence-final particle; 'indeed it is so', 'mark this']
entries.standardEnglish: no lexical equivalent; English renderings either add an archaic tag ('so it is', 'verily') or leave it unmarked
entries.wohChoice: rendered as a plain assertive English declarative with NO recurring lexical tag; 'zo yo' is preserved only in the transliteration line. The oracular force is carried by the declarative mood and the surrounding diction, not by a repeated English marker
entries.rationale: ぞよ ends most verses and is the single most pervasive register feature of the text, so its treatment is a standing convention rather than a per-verse call. The WoH translation renders it as an unmarked assertive declarative and keeps 'zo yo' in the transliteration only, because a recurring English tag ('so it is', 'verily I say') repeated across ~85 verses would read as pastiche and over-mark a particle that in the source is simply the default oracular cadence, not an emphatic addition to each sentence. This is a direct translation-technique decision: the particle has no lexical content to render, and the accuracy-preserving choice is to let the declarative mood carry the assertive force while documenting the particle here and in the transliteration so nothing is silently dropped. The alternative (a fixed rendered tag) is recorded as considered and rejected. Reference: S. E. Martin, A Reference Grammar of Japanese (Yale 1975), on sentence-final ぞ/よ; S. Makino & M. Tsutsui, A Dictionary of Basic Japanese Grammar, s.vv. ぞ, よ.

entries.source: 艮の金神 / 艮金神 (＝国常立尊)
entries.translit: Ushitora no Konjin / Ushitora Konjin (= Kunitokotachi-no-Mikoto)
entries.lemma: 艮の金神 (Ushitora no Konjin), the central theonym of the Ōmoto Shin'yu: Konjin, a Konjin-class calendrical/directional deity (traditionally a feared taboo-kami of unlucky directions), of the 艮 ushitora quarter — the northeast, the 'ox-tiger' direction (丑寅). Ōmoto reframes this feared directional kami as the wronged, banished, and now-returning primordial creator-kami, and at OSHIN-1:52 explicitly identifies him with 国常立尊 Kunitokotachi-no-Mikoto, the primordial earth-kami of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki
entries.literal: the Golden Deity (Konjin) of the Northeast (ushitora / ox-tiger direction)
entries.standardEnglish: descriptive renderings vary: 'the Golden Deity of the Northeast', 'Konjin of the ushitora quarter'
entries.wohChoice: retain the romanized proper name 'Ushitora no Konjin' with a gloss on first use (OSHIN-1:1), rather than descriptivizing it. At OSHIN-1:52 the identification with 国常立尊 is rendered by apposition of both romanized names ('Ushitora no Konjin, Kunitokotachi-no-Mikoto') without collapsing them, following the source's own apposition
entries.rationale: 艮の金神 is a proper theonym naming a specific being who is the divine speaker of the oracle, and retaining the romanized name with a gloss is the accuracy-preserving choice: a descriptive translation ('the Golden Deity of the Northeast') would obscure that this is a named deity with a fixed cultic identity, not a generic epithet. The gloss is philologically direct — 艮 (ushitora) is the northeast, the ox-tiger point of the traditional twelve-direction compass, and Konjin is the well-attested class of calendrical taboo-deity (see the Onmyōdō directional-kami literature) — and the OSHIN-1:52 apposition with 国常立尊 is likewise direct because the text itself states the equation (皆艮金神国常立尊の仕組). The WoH keeps the two names apposed rather than reducing one to a gloss of the other, so the reader sees the Ōmoto theological identification the source makes rather than a translator's harmonization. Named references: the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki (国常立尊 as the primordial kami); Nakayama Shigeru and standard Ōmoto studies (Deguchi Onisaburō's Reikai Monogatari framing of Ushitora no Konjin as the banished creator). NOTE: any further identification of this banished-and-returning creator-kami with the Wheel of Heaven Elohim frame is a separate, interpretive, speculative move — NOT made here; see the escalated proposal in chapter-1-editor-report.md.

entries.source: 三千世界 / 三ぜん世界
entries.lemma: 三千世界 (sanzen sekai), 'the three-thousand worlds' — the Buddhist trichiliocosm (Skt. trisāhasra-mahāsāhasra-lokadhātu, 三千大千世界), a cosmos of a billion world-systems, borrowed into Ōmoto cosmology to denote the entire manifest universe that is to be washed, rebuilt, and renewed
entries.literal: the three-thousand worlds / the three-thousandfold world-system
entries.standardEnglish: often naturalized to 'the whole universe' / 'all the world(s)'
entries.wohChoice: rendered literally, 'the three-thousand worlds', preserving the Buddhist technical register rather than naturalizing it to 'the whole universe'
entries.rationale: 三千世界 is a Buddhist cosmological technical term (the trichiliocosm of Abhidharma cosmology, the 三千大千世界) taken up by Ōmoto as the scope of the world-renewal, and the load-bearing decision is whether to render it literally or naturalize it. The WoH translation keeps the literal 'three-thousand worlds' so the Buddhist register — and the sense of a vast, multi-world cosmos rather than merely the terrestrial 'world' (世界 alone) — stays visible to the reader, cross-referenced in commentary to its Abhidharma source. This is marked inferred rather than direct because the literal rendering is a defensible interpretive choice about register preservation, not the only possible or consensus English (a naturalizing 'the whole universe' is a legitimate alternative that the WoH records and rejects). Named references: the Abhidharmakośa (Vasubandhu) trichiliocosm; the entry 三千大千世界 in the Bukkyō-go daijiten; the term's currency in Edo-period usage (e.g. the proverb 三千世界の烏を殺し).

entries.source: 立替へ立直し / 立替立直し / 世の立替
entries.lemma: 立替へ立直し (tatekae-tatenaoshi), Ōmoto's core eschatological program — literally a carpentry/building metaphor: 立替へ tatekae 'tearing down and rebuilding (a structure anew)' + 立直し tatenaoshi 'setting straight / re-erecting / making right again'. Occurs in full at OSHIN-1:7 and 1:56 and in the reduced form 世の立替 yo no tatekae 'the reconstruction of the world' at 1:14, 1:15, 1:50, 1:51
entries.partOfSpeech: Japanese compound verbal noun (technical eschatological term)
entries.standardEnglish: renderings vary: 'reconstruction and renewal', 'demolition and reconstruction', 'rebuilding and rectification'
entries.wohChoice: translated in the running text as 'reconstruction and renewal' (the full compound) and 'the reconstruction of the world' (the reduced 世の立替), rather than retained as a romanized compound; the carpentry metaphor is glossed in commentary
entries.rationale: 立替へ立直し is the signature eschatological term of the Ōmoto Shin'yu, a paired carpentry metaphor for pulling the corrupt world down and re-erecting it aright, and the decision is both retain-vs-translate and, if translating, which English pair. The WoH translation renders it 'reconstruction and renewal': 立替へ carries the 'tear down and rebuild' sense (the same 立て替える of rebuilding a house), and 立直し the 'set right again / restore to true' sense, so 'reconstruction and renewal' captures the destructive-then-restorative arc without the purely demolitionary tone of 'demolition and reconstruction'. This is marked inferred because the English pair is a defensible interpretive choice among several (the more literal 'rebuilding and rectification' and the romanized-with-gloss option are recorded and rejected), balancing readability against the metaphor's concreteness. Retaining a project-beginning-of-renewal sense (a rebuilding of an existing world, not an ex nihilo re-creation) is consistent with the source's building imagery. Reference: the term 立替え立直し in Ōmoto doctrinal literature (Deguchi Onisaburō, Reikai Monogatari); Nihon kokugo daijiten s.vv. 立替え, 立直し.

entries.lemma: 改心 (kaishin), the inner turning — reform/renewal of the heart — that Ōmoto demands of a soul before it can survive the tatekae; literally 'to reform (改) the heart (心)'. Occurs at OSHIN-1:43, 1:78, 1:81, 1:86
entries.literal: reform of the heart / change of heart
entries.wohChoice: rendered consistently as 'change of heart' (or the verb 'to change one's heart'), rather than 'repentance'
entries.rationale: 改心 in Ōmoto is the demanded inner reorientation that qualifies a soul to pass through the world-renewal, and the choice is between the penitentially loaded 'repentance' and the more neutral 'change of heart'. The WoH translation uses 'change of heart' because 'repentance' imports the Christian penitential-contrition frame (sin, confession, absolution) that the Japanese 改心 (literally 'reform the heart') does not carry — 改心 is about reforming one's disposition and casting off the old mind (cf. 1:43's 生れ赤児の心に立返る, 'turn back to the heart of a newborn babe'), not about penance for offenses. This is marked inferred because 'change of heart' is a defensible register choice rather than the only rendering (romanized kaishin-with-gloss, and 'reform of heart', are recorded alternatives), and because the weaker-but-neutral option is deliberately preferred over the stronger-but-freighted one on accuracy-before-connotation grounds. Reference: Nihon kokugo daijiten s.v. 改心; contrast 悔い改め (kuiaratame), the term used for Christian 'repentance' in Japanese Bible translation, which the source does NOT use.

entries.lemma: 神 (kami), the divine speaker throughout the oracle and the generic word for deity; plural 神々 (kamigami). In the Ōmoto Shin'yu the singular divine speaker is a specific named being (Ushitora no Konjin / Kunitokotachi, OSHIN-1:52) who nonetheless speaks within a polytheistic frame populated by many kami (神々様, 1:57) and guardian deities
entries.literal: kami / deity / god (singular or plural, indefinite as to number)
entries.wohChoice: rendered NEUTRALLY by the text's own theism: 'the kami' for the singular divine speaker (definite, not capitalized 'God'); 'the kami' / 'the deities' for the plural 神々; 'the deity' where English idiom needs it. NO Wheel-of-Heaven / Raëlian vocabulary ('Elohim' and the like) is introduced into the line
entries.rationale: 神 is the divine speaker of the entire oracle, and how it is rendered is the one genuinely lens-sensitive lexical decision in the text — the exact parallel of the Hidden Words b-h-y ruling. The WoH translation keeps it strictly neutral: 'the kami', preserving the Japanese word untranslated, because rendering it 'God' (capitalized, monotheizing) would misrepresent a specifically polytheistic frame in which the speaker is one named kami among many (神々様 'the many kami', 守護神 guardian deities, 諸国の神 'the kami of every land'), while 'the kami' keeps the definite specific reference without importing monotheist theology. Crucially, NO Elohim/Raëlian vocabulary is injected into the translated line: the resonance between Ōmoto's banished-and-returning creator-kami and the Wheel of Heaven frame is real and interesting, but it is comparative apparatus that belongs in commentary and the wiki, and any interpretive identification is claim_type=speculative and is escalated to the human reviewer (chapter-1-editor-report.md), not committed. Marked inferred rather than direct because the standing 'the kami' rendering is a deliberate register decision (untranslated over 'God'/'deity') applied context-sensitively, not a mechanical gloss. This entry governs the generic divine-speaker 神 throughout; the proper theonym 艮の金神 is handled by its own entry.

entries.lemma: 神国 (shinkoku), 'the land of the kami' — the theocratic-restorative order the oracle promises: a realm governed by the kami, enduring 'to the last generation'. Occurs at OSHIN-1:2, 1:10, 1:19, 1:39, 1:40, 1:65; related terms 神道 Shintō (1:3, retained) and 神世 kamiyo 'divine age' (1:70)
entries.literal: divine land / land of the kami / land of the gods
entries.standardEnglish: 'divine land', 'land of the gods', or the WWII-era-loaded 'divine nation'
entries.wohChoice: rendered 'divine land', NOT the ideologically loaded 'divine nation' of later State-Shintō nationalism; the pre-militarist 1892 dating is noted in commentary
entries.rationale: 神国 is a theologically weighty term that later became a slogan of State-Shintō ultranationalism (the wartime 'divine nation' / kami-no-kuni ideology), so the rendering choice carries real interpretive freight. The WoH translation uses 'divine land' rather than 'divine nation' because this 1892 provincial oracle predates the militarist appropriation of the term by a generation, and its sense here is theocratic-restorative — a land the kami governs and sustains (神が構わな行けぬ国, 1:3) — rather than the modern nation-state nationalism 'divine nation' would anachronistically import. This is marked inferred because 'divine land' is a defensible reading against the loaded alternative, and the decision turns on historical contextualization (pre- vs post-militarist usage) that belongs in the apparatus; the alternative 'land of the kami' is recorded and is near-equivalent. Named reference: standard treatments of the shinkoku shisō and its Meiji-to-Shōwa transformation (e.g. Kuroda Toshio on shinkoku thought); the 1892 dating is fixed by the source (Meiji 25).

entries.source: 神柱 / 神の柱 ・ 守護神 ・ 守護人
entries.translit: kamibashira / kami no hashira · shugojin · shugonin
entries.lemma: the Ōmoto agent-hierarchy: 神柱 / 神の柱 (kamibashira / kami no hashira), 'divine pillar(s)' — not physical pillars but the human mediums, leaders, and rival founders through whom kami work (1:14, 1:15, 1:51); 守護神 (shugojin), 'guardian deity' — the tutelary kami assigned to persons/places and summoned to service (1:40, 1:53, 1:56, 1:57); 守護人 (shugonin), 'guardian' — the human guardians who 'stand over' Japan (1:66). Plural 神々様 (kamigami-sama) 'the many kami' (1:57)
entries.standardEnglish: these are frequently merged into 'guardian spirit(s)' / 'divine pillar(s)'
entries.wohChoice: kept distinct: 神柱 = 'divine pillar', 守護神 = 'guardian deity', 守護人 = 'guardian'. shugojin (deity) and shugonin (person) are NOT merged
entries.rationale: The oracle deploys three related but distinct agent-terms, and English renderings routinely collapse them into an undifferentiated 'guardian spirit'. The WoH translation keeps them distinct: 神柱 'divine pillar' for the human mediums/leaders (and rival founders) figured as pillars through which the divine acts; 守護神 'guardian deity' for the tutelary kami; and 守護人 'guardian' for the human guardians of 1:66 — the 神/人 (deity/person) distinction between shugojin and shugonin being marked in the source itself and worth preserving. This is marked inferred because the three-way English mapping is a defensible disambiguation rather than the only rendering (merging shugojin and shugonin is a recorded, rejected alternative), and because 神柱's metaphor (human agents as 'pillars') is an interpretive reading of a term that could be flattened to 'leader'. The distinction lets the reader track Ōmoto's claim that many 'divine pillars' arise worldwide (1:51) while the guardian deities are gathered and assigned service at Ayabe (1:53). Reference: Nihon kokugo daijiten s.vv. 神柱, 守護神; the 御柱/hashira counter for kami in Shintō usage.

entries.lemma: the lacuna/redaction markers ○○○［ (and ○○［, てん○○［) that appear at OSHIN-1:23, 1:29, 1:39, 1:71 — circles standing for characters the reikaimonogatari.net witness leaves illegible or suppressed in the fude (brush-written) original, with the bracket ［ marking the opening of the affected span
entries.standardEnglish: editorial conventions vary: bracketed ellipsis […], asterisks, or a footnote
entries.wohChoice: preserve the markers verbatim (○○○[) in BOTH the Japanese and the English line, rather than substituting a bracketed ellipsis or a footnote, so the redaction is visible and not silently smoothed over
entries.rationale: The source text carries lacuna/redaction glyphs (circles plus an opening bracket) at four places where the witness could not or would not render the fude characters, and the house-convention decision is how to represent them in the English. The WoH convention preserves them verbatim in both languages because they are a feature of the transmitted text — visible evidence that the oracle's original brush-writing has illegible or withheld spans — and substituting a normalized '[…]' or relegating them to a footnote would erase that evidentiary surface from the reading line. This is a direct editorial/house-style fact rather than an interpretive reading: it documents a rendering convention, not a claim about what the missing characters were. The alternatives (bracketed ellipsis; footnote-only) are recorded and rejected in favor of maximal transparency, consistent with the project's preference for auditable, non-smoothed text.

entries.source: 金輪王 ・ 高天原 ・ 竜門館 ・ 生神
entries.lemma: the mythic/cosmological title-and-toponym set of the Ayabe eschatology: 金輪王 (konrin'ō), the 'Golden-Wheel King', highest cakravartin (wheel-turning universal monarch) of Buddhist cosmology, here the eschatological world-ruler seated at Ayabe (1:49); 高天原 (Takamagahara), the 'High Plain of Heaven' of Shintō myth (1:53, 1:71); 竜門館 (Ryūmonkan), 'Dragon-Gate Hall', the Ayabe sanctuary building (1:53, 1:71); 生神 (ikigami), a 'living kami' — a human being in whom a kami is manifestly present (1:71). Related: 地場 jiba 'sacred ground' (1:50)
entries.literal: Golden-Wheel King; High Plain of Heaven; Dragon-Gate Hall; living kami
entries.standardEnglish: mixed practice: cakravartin titles and Takamagahara are variously translated or transliterated
entries.wohChoice: a hybrid retain-vs-translate policy: the title 金輪王 is TRANSLATED 'Golden-Wheel King' (its cakravartin sense being legible in English); the named mythic/place entities are RETAINED romanized with a gloss — Takamagahara ('High Plain of Heaven'), Ryūmonkan ('Dragon-Gate Hall'), ikigami ('living kami')
entries.rationale: This cluster names the mythic apparatus of the Ayabe eschatology, and a single blanket policy fails: the title 金輪王 has a legible English equivalent (the Golden-Wheel cakravartin, the supreme wheel-turning monarch of Buddhist cosmology), so translating it 'Golden-Wheel King' conveys sense a bare transliteration would hide, whereas 高天原 and 竜門館 are proper names/loci that function as fixed points in the cosmology and read best retained with a gloss (translating Takamagahara as 'the High Plain of Heaven' every time would over-domesticate a proper name). 生神 'living kami' is retained-with-gloss because it is a technical status-term (a human vessel of a kami) whose force 'living god' would overstate in English. This is marked inferred because the retain-vs-translate line and the 'Golden-Wheel King' rendering are defensible scholarly choices, not the only ones (fully-translate and fully-romanize are recorded alternatives). Named references: the cakravartin / 転輪聖王 in Buddhist cosmology (the golden-wheel 金輪 being the highest of the four wheel-kings); the Kojiki Takamagahara; the Bukkyō-go daijiten s.v. 金輪王.

entries.source: 大本 / 世の本 / 世の根
entries.translit: Ōmoto / ō-moto · yo no moto · yo no ne
entries.lemma: 大本, carrying a live double sense: (a) the proper name of the movement / sacred site at Ayabe (綾部の大本, 1:17, 1:40, 1:53, 1:56); (b) the common noun 'the great origin / foundation' (昔の大本 'the great origin of old', 1:39). Related origin-nouns: 世の本 yo no moto 'the origin of the world' (1:53, 1:56, 1:59), 世の根 yo no ne 'the root of the world' (1:53)
entries.partOfSpeech: Japanese proper name / common noun (double sense)
entries.literal: the great origin / great foundation; (as proper name) Ōmoto
entries.standardEnglish: 'Ōmoto' as the movement name; 'the great origin/source' as the common noun
entries.wohChoice: split by sense: 'the Ōmoto' where 大本 names the movement/sacred site at Ayabe; 'the great origin' where it is the common noun (1:39); 世の本 'the origin of the world', 世の根 'the root of the world'. The 1892 anachronism (the movement not yet formally named) is noted in commentary
entries.rationale: 大本 is genuinely ambiguous in the source between the eventual proper name of the movement (the Ayabe 大本) and the ordinary common noun 'great origin/foundation', and the two senses sit side by side (the site 綾部の大本 at 1:40 vs 昔の大本 'the great origin of old' at 1:39). The WoH translation splits them by context — 'the Ōmoto' for the site/movement, 'the great origin' for the common noun — because collapsing everything to the proper name would be anachronistic (in 1892 the movement was not yet formally constituted or named Ōmoto, so the site-sense is proleptic) while collapsing everything to the common noun would erase the incipient place-name the oracle is establishing. This is marked inferred because the sense-split is an interpretive judgment call verse by verse (a defensible reading, with 'always the Ōmoto' and 'always the Great Origin' recorded as rejected alternatives), and because flagging the proper-name usage as proleptic is a historical contextualization proper to the apparatus. Reference: the history of the naming of Ōmoto (大本), formally organized after 1892; Nihon kokugo daijiten s.v. 大本 (おおもと) 'great origin/foundation'.

entries.lemma: 出口直 (Deguchi Nao), the prophetess through whom the oracle is written (named in full at OSHIN-1:45). At 1:91 and 1:92 the single character 直 functions doubly as her personal name (Nao) and as the adverb 直 (nao / sunao, 'directly, truly, straightforwardly') — a deliberate wordplay
entries.wohChoice: read 直 as the personal name 'Nao' at 1:91 and 1:92 (the kami's lament for its medium), with the co-present adverbial sense ('truly/directly') carried in the same clause and noted in commentary
entries.rationale: The character 直 is the prophetess's name (Deguchi Nao, spelled out at 1:45) and simultaneously the common adverb nao/sunao 'directly, truly', and at 1:91–92 the text exploits both at once — a pun the translator must adjudicate. The WoH reads it primarily as the name 'Nao' because the surrounding clauses are explicitly about the medium's burden and suffering (余り大望な取次さして在る 'so grand a mediumship has been laid [on her]'; 直の悔しさ、残念さ 'Nao's mortification and regret'), making the personal-lament reading the governing one; the adverbial 'truly/directly' sense is real and is carried by the English in the same breath ('truly a grievous thing') and glossed. This is marked inferred because resolving a deliberate pun toward one pole is an interpretive decision (the name-reading over the adverb-reading), with the fully-explicit both-senses rendering recorded as an alternative. Reading these closing verses as the kami's lament for Nao is consistent with the biographical frame of the founding fude. Reference: the biography of Deguchi Nao (Ōmoto founder, 1837–1918); the 直/なほ orthography in historical kana.

entries.source: 獣類 / 獣の世 ・ 外国 / 外国人 ・ 盲目聾 ・ 悪魔
entries.translit: jūrui / kemono no yo · gaikoku / gaikokujin · mekura tsunbo · akuma
entries.lemma: the sensitive-register vocabulary of the 1892 oracle: 獣類 jūrui / 獣の世 kemono no yo 'beasts / a world of beasts' (1:4, 1:5) and 悪魔 akuma 'devils' (1:4) applied to the foreign nations; the xenophobic 外国 / 外国人 gaikoku(jin) 'foreign countries / foreigners' rhetoric (1:4, 1:6, 1:25, 1:30); and the now-strongly-derogatory 盲目聾 mekura tsunbo 'blind and deaf' (1:24), used metaphorically of the spiritually unseeing
entries.literal: beasts / world of beasts; foreign countries / foreigners; blind and deaf; devils
entries.standardEnglish: n/a (editorial-policy entry, not a single-lemma rendering)
entries.wohChoice: ACCURACY-FIRST: render the literal English in every case, neither softening nor amplifying; add scholarly notes.official at the affected verses contextualizing (the pre-militarist 1892 dating; the oracular idiom; the metaphorical target). The text is documented, not endorsed; it is not sanitized and it is not amplified
entries.rationale: The 1892 oracle contains xenophobic ('world of beasts', 'nothing but devils', the foreigner rhetoric) and now-derogatory ableist ('blind and deaf') vocabulary, and the project's accuracy-first policy governs: the WoH keeps the literal English rather than softening it, because sanitizing a primary source would misrepresent what the text says, while amplifying or foregrounding it would editorialize. This entry documents that policy decision and its paired obligation — scholarly framing in the apparatus (notes.official at 1:4 and 1:24) noting that the text is a pre-militarist provincial oracle predating the Sino-Japanese War and the State-Shintō absorption of this register; that 'world of beasts' is the oracle's idiom for a moral order it judges predatory (turned on Japan itself at 1:5); and that 盲目聾 is figurative for the spiritually heedless (the teacup-at-the-well image). This is claim_type=direct: it records an editorial-handling fact and a literal-rendering decision, not an interpretive reading of the lemmata. The framing is contextualization, not endorsement; the vocabulary reflects 1892 usage. Cross-reference: chapter-1-editor-report.md (sensitive-register handling).

entries.source: 水晶魂 ・ 霊魂の改め ・ 心魂
entries.lemma: the soul-purification vocabulary of the second fude: 水晶魂 (suishō-damashii), the 'crystal soul' — the purified, transparent soul selected to survive the tatekae (1:76); 霊魂の改め (reikon no aratame), the 'sifting/examination of souls', 改め = winnowing/inspection (1:76); 霊魂 reikon 'soul' (1:85); 心魂 shinkon 'heart-and-soul' (1:86)
entries.literal: crystal soul; examination/winnowing of souls; heart-and-soul
entries.wohChoice: retain the metaphor: 水晶魂 = 'crystal soul'; render 霊魂の改め = 'the sifting of souls' (改め as examination/winnowing); 霊魂 = 'soul', 心魂 = 'heart and soul'
entries.rationale: The second fude introduces Ōmoto's soul-selection doctrine, in which the 'crystal soul' (the soul made transparent/pure) is chosen to pass through the world-renewal while others are examined and sifted. The WoH retains the concrete metaphor 'crystal soul' (over a paraphrase like 'soul of crystal purity') because the mineral image is doctrinally load-bearing in Ōmoto and legible in English, and renders 霊魂の改め 'the sifting of souls' — 改め carrying the sense of inspection/winnowing (as of accounts or persons) that 'selecting out the crystal souls' (水晶魂を選り抜いて) in the same verse makes concrete. This is marked inferred because 'crystal soul' + 'sifting' is a defensible rendering among alternatives ('examination/reckoning of souls'; 'soul of crystal purity + reform of souls' are recorded and rejected), preserving both the metaphor and the selective-judgment sense. Reference: the mitama (魂) and soul-refinement vocabulary of Ōmoto doctrine; Nihon kokugo daijiten s.vv. 水晶, 改め.

entries.translit: [RMN-os004 / RMN-os013 witnesses; 38/93 exact match; single-edition pass pending]
entries.lemma: the collation-witness framework for the Ōmoto Shin'yu WoH source: the reikaimonogatari.net (霊界物語ネット / Onido) e-text is the working transcription, drawn from witnesses RMN-os004 (Meiji 25 old-cal. 1st month, verses 1–75) and RMN-os013 (old-cal. 5th month 5th day, verses 76–93), rendered de-furigana'd. Machine collation after furigana-stripping matched 38/93 verses EXACTLY; the remainder differ by orthographic variants (kana/kanji choices such as 三ぜん/三千) and, at OSHIN-1:1, the sense-bearing variant 一同 ichidō ('all together') vs the witness's 一度 ichido ('at one stroke/at one time'). A single-edition philological pass against an authoritative Ōmoto Shin'yu edition is PENDING before sign-off
entries.literal: the reikaimonogatari.net working transcription, its partial (38/93) exact match, and the retained 一同/一度 variant
entries.standardEnglish: an authoritative printed Ōmoto Shin'yu edition (Deguchi Onisaburō's compiled text) as the reference control
entries.wohChoice: the reikaimonogatari.net transcription is retained as the working source and translated as printed; the ja fields are kept AS-IS. At OSHIN-1:1 the printed 一同 ('all together') is followed in the English over the witness's 一度 ('at one stroke'); the variant is recorded here and in commentary. Verification status is held at 'witness-confirmed-collation-partial'; a single-edition philological pass is flagged as pending
entries.rationale: The WoH source is a de-furigana'd transcription of the reikaimonogatari.net Ōmoto Shin'yu e-text, and machine collation after furigana-stripping matched only 38 of 93 verses exactly, with the remainder differing by orthographic variants between this transcription and the witness rendering — differences of edition/orthography, not content errors. This entry records that collation state so the English is auditable and the verification status is not overstated: it is 'witness-confirmed-collation-partial', and a human philological pass against a single authoritative edition is required before final sign-off to settle the orthographic variants and lock verse numbering. The one variant with a real sense difference is at OSHIN-1:1 — printed 一同 ichidō ('all together, all as one') vs the witness's 一度 ichido ('at one stroke, at one time') — where the WoH follows the printed text ('all together') and records the witness alternative rather than silently adopting it. This is claim_type=direct: it documents a collation/editorial fact and a text-fidelity decision, not an interpretive reading. Named reference: reikaimonogatari.net (霊界物語ネット / Onido) witnesses RMN-os004 and RMN-os013; project policy (strategy-library-acquisition.md) requiring pre-sign-off verification against an authoritative edition, still pending.
